diagnostics.notes: Both claims concern triglyceride changes under carbohydrate-manipulating diets; extraction fields match their sources. Side A: within-group increase in triglycerides after 3 weeks of an HC/low-fat diet (76 to 104 mg/dL, p = 0.005). Side B: clinically meaningful improvement (reduction) in triglycerides with a low-carbohydrate, energy-restricted diet over 12 weeks (p < 0.0001), though the abstract does not specify whether this is within-group or between-group. Directions are genuinely opposite. The abstracts themselves supply a concrete explanatory difference: side A tested a high-carbohydrate/low-fat diet in healthy physically active adults, while side B tested a low-carbohydrate (<50 g), energy-restricted (~850-1100 kcal/day) diet in people with type 2 diabetes. The opposing carbohydrate composition of the interventions and differing populations are text-supported on both sides and could explain the opposite triglyceride directions.

source_evidence.quote: while triglycerides significantly increased (76 ± 38 mg/dL at baseline to 104 ± 44 mg/dL; p = 0.005)
These reductions occurred concurrently with clinically meaningful improvements in hemoglobin A1C, anthropometrics, blood pressure, and triglycerides (all p < 0.0001).
The present study investigated the impact of a three-week period of HC/low-fat (HC) diet followed by a three-week wash-out-phase and subsequent LC diet
low-carbohydrate (<50 g), energy-restricted diet (~850-1100 kcal/day; Pharm-TCR; n = 98)

verdict.label: apparent_contradiction
verdict.rationale: Both abstracts report triglyceride changes under carbohydrate-altering diets, so the outcome and general exposure domain are comparable. Side A reports a significant within-group increase in triglycerides after three weeks of a high-carbohydrate/low-fat diet (76 to 104 mg/dL; p = 0.005), while side B reports a significant improvement (reduction) in triglycerides with a low-carbohydrate, energy-restricted diet over 12 weeks (p < 0.0001). The directions are opposite, but each abstract textually describes a different intervention and population: an HC/low-fat diet in physically active adults versus a low-carbohydrate (<50 g), energy-restricted diet in people with type 2 diabetes. This supported difference in the dietary intervention (and population) plausibly explains the opposing triglyceride findings, so the pair is classified as apparent_contradiction rather than contradictory.
